cards.title: Hello, Python
cards.html:
This unit is for two kinds of people: complete beginners, and anyone who has coded before but can't remember how any of it goes. Either way it assumes nothing and starts from the very first line of Python.

New to coding? Read slowly and type the examples out yourself rather than copy-pasting; typing is how the syntax sticks. Coming back to it? Skim the cards and let the questions show you what you've forgotten. Either way the questions are small on purpose: lots of quick reps beat one big exercise.

The coding questions in Unit 0 work like classic beginner programs: read with input(), print the answer, and the tests feed in the input and check what you printed.

cards.title: Variables
cards.html:
A variable is a name pointing at a value. = means "make this name point at this value", not "equals".

age = 19
name = "Alex"
height = 1.82
is_student = True
age = age + 1      # read age (19), add 1, point age at 20

The four basic types: int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text, in quotes), bool (True / False). type(x) tells you which one you have.

cards.title: Printing
cards.html:
print("hello")
print("age:", age)            # commas add a space between items
print(f"{name} is {age}")     # f-string: anything in {} gets filled in
print(f"{3.14159:.2f}")       # 3.14  (2 decimal places)

cards.title: Reading input
cards.html:
input() waits for a line of text and gives it back as a string, always. If you want a number, convert it:

n = int(input())       # whole number
x = float(input())     # decimal
word = input()         # leave text as text

Forgetting int() is the most common Unit 0 bug: "3" + "4" is "34".

cards.title: Arithmetic
cards.html:
7 + 2    # 9
7 - 2    # 5
7 * 2    # 14
7 / 2    # 3.5   always gives a float
7 // 2   # 3     whole-number division (rounds down)
7 % 2    # 1     remainder
7 ** 2   # 49    power

// and % come up constantly: n % 10 is the last digit of n, n // 10 removes it, and n % 2 == 0 checks for even.

x = 10
x = x * 2
x = x // 3
print(x, x % 4)
Predict it: what does this print? Decide, then click.

6 2. x goes 10 → 20 → 6 (20 // 3 is 6), and 6 % 4 is 2.

cards.title: Making decisions
cards.html: Programs make decisions with if. Python uses indentation (4 spaces) to show what's inside the if. There are no braces like in Java or C.

cards.title: if / elif / else
cards.html:
mark = int(input())

if mark >= 70:
    print("A")
elif mark >= 55:        # only checked if the line above was False
    print("B")
else:                   # runs if nothing above matched
    print("F")
print("done")           # not indented: always runs

Python checks top to bottom and runs only the first branch that's True. That's why order matters.

cards.title: Comparisons and combining them
cards.html:
a == b    # equal (one = assigns, two == compares)
a != b    # not equal
a < b, a <= b, a > b, a >= b

if age >= 18 and age < 65:
if day == 6 or day == 7:
if not finished:
if 18 <= age < 65:      # Python allows chained comparisons

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.html:
• Forgetting the colon at the end of if ...: (SyntaxError).
  • Using = instead of == in a condition.
  • Writing separate ifs when you meant elif. Several ifs can all run; elif stops at the first match.
  • Wrong boundary: is 70 an A or a B? Decide whether you need > or >=.
n = 15
if n % 3 == 0:
    print("fizz")
if n % 5 == 0:
    print("buzz")
elif n % 3 == 0:
    print("three")
Predict it: what does this print?

fizz then buzz. The first if is separate, so it runs. The second if is also True, so its elif is skipped.

skills.name: and, or, and the order of checks

levels.title: While loops
levels.short: Start, condition, step; tracing by hand

cards.title: While loops
cards.html: While loops are where most people get stuck at first, and the first thing to go when you are out of practice, so this level goes slowly.

cards.title: The shape of every while loop
cards.html:
A while loop needs three things. Get used to looking for all three:

i = 1               # 1. START: set up the variable before the loop
while i <= 5:       # 2. CONDITION: keep going while this is True
    print(i)
    i = i + 1       # 3. STEP: change the variable so the condition eventually fails
print("after")

Python checks the condition, runs the indented body, goes back up, checks again. When the condition is False it skips to the first line after the loop.

cards.title: Trace it by hand
cards.html:
When a loop confuses you, make a table: one row per time round the loop. This is the single best habit for getting back into "programming mode".

total = 0
i = 1
while i <= 4:
    total = total + i
    i = i + 1
print(total)
check i <= 4 total after i after
1 ≤ 4 yes 1 2
2 ≤ 4 yes 3 3
3 ≤ 4 yes 6 4
4 ≤ 4 yes 10 5
5 ≤ 4 no, stop

Prints 10.

cards.title: The three ways a while loop goes wrong
cards.html:
1. No step (forgot i = i + 1): the condition never changes, and the loop runs forever. In this app it gets stopped after 10 seconds.
  2. Off by one: < vs <=, or starting at 0 vs 1. Trace the first and last time round to check.
  3. Step in the wrong place: i = i + 1 indented under an if only runs sometimes.

cards.title: Loops that run "until something happens"
cards.html:
Not every loop counts. Sometimes you don't know how many times it'll go round:

line = input()           # read the first one before the loop
while line != "end":
    print("got", line)
    line = input()       # read the next one as the LAST step

Now trace this one in your head before you click:

n = 1
while n < 100:
    n = n * 3
print(n)
Predict it: what does this print?

243. n goes 1 → 3 → 9 → 27 → 81 → 243. The check happens before each round, so 81 < 100 lets it go round once more.

cards.title: break
cards.html:
break jumps out of the loop immediately. Setting i = len(s) to force a loop to end works, but break is the proper way.

while True:          # loop "forever"...
    word = input()
    if word == "stop":
        break        # ...until this
    print(word)

levels.title: For loops & range
levels.short: range, looping over things, break, continue

cards.title: For loops & range
cards.html: A for loop goes through things one at a time. Use it when you know what you're looping over: a range of numbers, the characters of a string, the items of a list. Python handles the start, the condition and the step for you, so you can't forget the step.

cards.title: for with range
cards.html:
for i in range(5):          # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4   (5 numbers, stops BEFORE 5)
for i in range(1, 6):       # 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
for i in range(0, 10, 2):   # 0, 2, 4, 6, 8   (third number is the step)
for i in range(5, 0, -1):   # 5, 4, 3, 2, 1   (counting down)

The stop number is never included. To go up to n, write range(1, n + 1).

These two do exactly the same thing:

i = 1
while i <= 5:
    print(i)
    i = i + 1

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)

cards.title: for over a string or a list
cards.html:
for ch in "hey":
    print(ch)           # h, e, y on separate lines

for name in ["ann", "bob"]:
    print("hi", name)

When you need the position too, loop over range(len(s)) and use s[i]. (In Unit 1 you'll learn enumerate, which is neater.)

cards.title: while or for?
cards.html:
• Know how many times, or looping over something? for.
  • Looping until a condition changes (until "end", until n is 1, two pointers meeting)? while.

cards.title: break and continue
cards.html:
break leaves the loop. continue skips the rest of this round and goes on to the next.

for i in range(1, 8):
    if i % 3 == 0:
        continue
    if i == 6:
        break
    print(i)
Predict it: what does this print?

1 2 4 5 7, one per line. 3 and 6 are skipped by continue before the break check, so the break never fires.

cards.title: print on one line
cards.html: print(x, end=" ") ends with a space instead of a new line. Call print() once at the end to finish the line.

cards.title: Strings
cards.html: Strings are sequences of characters. Almost everything here works on lists too, so it pays off twice.

cards.title: Indexing
cards.html:
s = "python"
#    012345      positions start at 0
s[0]       # "p"
s[5]       # "n"
s[-1]      # "n"   negative counts from the end
len(s)     # 6     so the last index is len(s) - 1
s[6]       # IndexError: there is no position 6

cards.title: Slicing
cards.html:
s[start:stop] takes from start up to, but not including, stop. Leave a side empty to mean "from the beginning" or "to the end".

s[0:3]     # "pyt"
s[2:]      # "thon"
s[:2]      # "py"
s[::-1]    # "nohtyp"   (step -1 = backwards)

cards.title: Useful string methods
cards.html:
"Hi There".lower()          # "hi there"
"hi".upper()                # "HI"
"  x  ".strip()             # "x"
"a b  c".split()            # ["a", "b", "c"]   (splits on any spaces)
"-".join(["a", "b", "c"])   # "a-b-c"
"banana".count("a")         # 3
"banana".replace("a", "o")  # "bonono"
"7".isdigit(), "x".isalpha(), "Q".isupper()
"an" in "banana"            # True

cards.title: Strings can't be changed
cards.html:
s[0] = "P" is an error. Strings are immutable. Build a new string instead:

result = ""
for ch in s:
    result = result + ch.upper()

Check yourself:

s = "Hello, World"
print(s[7:], s[-5:-2], len(s.split()))
Predict it: what does this print?

World Wor 2. Index 7 is "W". s[-5:-2] is positions 7, 8, 9. Splitting on spaces gives two words.

cards.title: Lists
cards.html: A list holds many values in order. It's the thing you'll use most on LeetCode.

cards.title: Making and using lists
cards.html:
nums = [4, 8, 15]
nums[0]          # 4      same indexing as strings
nums[-1]         # 15
len(nums)        # 3
nums.append(16)  # add to the end: [4, 8, 15, 16]
nums[1] = 99     # lists CAN be changed: [4, 99, 15, 16]
nums.pop()       # removes and returns the last item (16)
8 in nums        # False now

cards.title: Building a list from input
cards.html:
nums = []                        # start empty
for i in range(5):
    nums.append(int(input()))    # read 5 numbers into it

Or from one line of space-separated numbers:

nums = [int(x) for x in input().split()]

(That bracket syntax is a list comprehension. Unit 1 covers it properly.)

cards.title: Looping over a list
cards.html:
total = 0
for x in nums:
    total = total + x

for i in range(len(nums)):    # when you need the index
    print(i, nums[i])

cards.title: Built-ins worth knowing
cards.html:
sum(nums), max(nums), min(nums)
sorted(nums)          # new sorted list
nums.sort()           # sorts nums itself
nums[::-1]            # reversed copy

Some questions ask you to do these by hand first. That's deliberate: on LeetCode you constantly write "keep track of the best so far" loops that max can't do for you.

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)
Predict it: what does this print?

[1, 2, 3, 4]. b = a doesn't copy the list; both names point at the same list. Use b = a[:] for a copy. This catches everyone at least once.

levels.title: Functions
levels.short: def, return, and why LeetCode needs them

cards.title: Functions
cards.html: Last level of Unit 0, and the bridge to everything after it. On LeetCode you never use input() or print(). You write a function, LeetCode calls it with the input, and it checks what you return.

cards.title: def and return
cards.html:
def add(a, b):        # a and b are parameters
    return a + b      # send the answer back to whoever called it

result = add(3, 4)    # 7
print(add(10, 5))     # 15

return ends the function immediately. Anything after it in that function doesn't run.

cards.title: print is not return
cards.html:
def bad_add(a, b):
    print(a + b)      # shows 7 on screen...

x = bad_add(3, 4)     # ...but x is None, because nothing was returned

If a test says it expected 7 but got None, you printed instead of returning, or forgot the return.

cards.title: From script style to function style
cards.html:
# script style
n = int(input())
total = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    total = total + i
print(total)

# from now on
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + i
    return total

Same logic. The input becomes a parameter and the print becomes a return.

cards.title: Returning early
cards.html:
def first_negative(nums):
    for x in nums:
        if x < 0:
            return x      # found it, stop the whole function
    return None           # only reached if the loop finished without finding one

This "return inside the loop, fallback after it" shape shows up in loads of LeetCode problems.

One last check:

def f(n):
    if n > 10:
        return "big"
    return "small"
    print("hello")

print(f(3), f(30))
Predict it: what does this print?

small big. print("hello") never runs, because return always happens first.

From here on, every coding question is a function with tests, the same as LeetCode. After this unit's boss, Unit 1 sharpens all of this into the Python interviews use.

levels.title: The Gatekeeper
levels.short: Everything from Unit 0 at once: loops, decisions, strings and functions.

cards.title: Python re-entry
cards.html: Unit 0 got the basics moving again. This level tightens them into the Python people actually write in interviews: shortcuts that replace the manual index loops and extra variables beginners tend to write. If a line below looks unfamiliar, that's the bit to practise.

cards.title: Loops without manual indexes
cards.html:
Beginner code is full of i = 0; while i < len(s): ...; i = i + 1. In Python you almost never need that.

for ch in s:                      # just the items
for i in range(n):                # 0 .. n-1
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):    # n-1 down to 0
for i, ch in enumerate(s):        # index and item together
for a, b in zip(xs, ys):          # walk two lists in step

Keep while for when the step isn't fixed: two pointers, binary search, "keep going until". To leave a loop early, use break, or return inside a function. Setting i = len(s) to force an exit is a workaround from languages without break.

cards.title: Slicing
cards.html:
s[start:stop:step], stop excluded. Works on lists, strings and tuples, and always makes a copy.

s[::-1]     # reversed
a[1:]       # all but the first
a[:k]       # first k
a[-1]       # last item
b = a[:]    # shallow copy of a list

cards.title: Comprehensions
cards.html:
squares = [x * x for x in nums]
evens   = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]
index   = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(nums)}
unique  = {x % 10 for x in nums}
grid    = [[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]

cards.title: Functions return, they don't print
cards.html:
LeetCode calls your function and checks the return value. Get out of the input()/print() habit from beginner exercises.

def min_max(nums):
    return min(nums), max(nums)   # returns a tuple

lo, hi = min_max([3, 1, 4])       # unpacking
a, b = b, a                       # swap, no temp variable

cards.title: Things you'll use every day
cards.html:
x if cond else y                  # ternary
any(x < 0 for x in nums)          # True if at least one
all(x > 0 for x in nums)
max(words, key=len)               # longest word
sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: p[1]) # sort by second item
ch.isdigit(), ch.isalpha(), ch.isupper(), ch.lower()
" ".join(words)                   # list of strings -> one string
s.split()                         # string -> words
ord("a"), chr(97)                 # char <-> code; ord(ch) - ord("a") gives 0..25
float("inf"), float("-inf")       # starting values for min/max searches
divmod(17, 5)                     # (3, 2)

Truthiness: empty list, empty string, 0, None are all falsy. if not stack: is the normal way to check for empty.

Coming up: classic beginner programs, rewritten the Python way.

cards.title: The interview toolkit
cards.html: LeetCode in Python is mostly about picking the right built-in container. Know what each operation costs, because the cost is usually what makes a solution pass or fail.

cards.title: What things cost
cards.html:
Operation list dict / set deque
index a[i] O(1) — O(n)
x in ... O(n) O(1) O(n)
append / add at end O(1) O(1) O(1)
pop from end O(1) — O(1)
pop from front O(n) — O(1)
insert at front O(n) — O(1)
sort O(n log n) — —

The two rows that catch people: x in list inside a loop turns O(n) into O(n²), and list.pop(0) is O(n). If you need a queue, use a deque.

cards.title: collections
cards.html:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque

Counter("hello")              # Counter({'l': 2, 'h': 1, 'e': 1, 'o': 1})
Counter(nums).most_common(2)  # [(value, count), ...]

graph = defaultdict(list)     # missing keys start as []
graph[a].append(b)
count = defaultdict(int)      # missing keys start as 0
count[x] += 1

q = deque([start])
q.append(x); q.popleft()      # BFS queue, both O(1)

cards.title: heapq (min-heap on a plain list)
cards.html:
import heapq
heapq.heapify(nums)            # O(n), in place
heapq.heappush(h, x)           # O(log n)
smallest = heapq.heappop(h)    # O(log n)
h[0]                           # peek at the smallest
heapq.heappush(h, -x)          # max-heap trick: store negatives
heapq.heappush(h, (dist, node))  # tuples compare by first item
heapq.nlargest(k, nums), heapq.nsmallest(k, nums, key=...)

cards.title: bisect (binary search on a sorted list)
cards.html:
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
bisect_left(a, x)    # first index i with a[i] >= x
bisect_right(a, x)   # first index i with a[i] > x

cards.title: Sorting
cards.html: a.sort() sorts in place and returns None. sorted(a) returns a new list. For multiple criteria, use a tuple key: key=lambda p: (-p.score, p.name).

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• grid = [[0] * n] * m makes m references to the same row. Use [[0] * n for _ in range(m)].
  • def f(x, seen=[]): the default list is shared between calls. Use seen=None.
  • s += ch in a loop can be O(n²). Collect pieces in a list and "".join(parts).
  • -7 // 2 == -4 (floors). For truncation toward zero, use int(-7 / 2).
  • Recursion limit is about 1000 deep. Deep DFS on big inputs might need sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6) or an explicit stack.
  • Strings are immutable. To edit characters, chars = list(s), edit, then "".join(chars).

cards.title: Big-O & how to approach
cards.html: Every LeetCode problem gives you constraints. They tell you which complexity the intended solution has before you've thought about the problem.

cards.title: Read the constraints first
cards.html:
n up to Target complexity Usually means
10–12 O(n!) permutations, brute force
20–25 O(2ⁿ) subsets, backtracking, bitmasks
100–500 O(n³) triple loop, interval DP
1,000–5,000 O(n²) double loop, 2D DP
10⁵–10⁶ O(n log n) or O(n) sorting, heap, hashing, two pointers, sliding window
10⁹ or more O(log n) or O(1) binary search, maths

Rule of thumb: Python handles about 10⁷ simple operations per second. If n = 10⁵, O(n²) = 10¹⁰, which will time out.

cards.title: Complexity, quickly
cards.html:
• One loop over n: O(n). Nested loops over n: O(n²).
  • Halving each step (binary search): O(log n).
  • Sorting: O(n log n). If you sort first, the whole solution is at least that.
  • Recursion: (number of calls) × (work per call). Fibonacci without memo is O(2ⁿ); with memo, O(n).
  • Hidden costs: x in list, slicing, list.pop(0), s + t on strings. Each is O(n).
  • Space counts too: a set of everything seen is O(n) extra.

cards.title: The routine (use it on every problem)
cards.html:
1. Restate it and walk through the given examples by hand. Invent an edge case: empty input, one element, all duplicates, negatives.
  2. Say the brute force and its complexity. In interviews, saying it out loud is worth points.
  3. Find the waste. What does the brute force recompute or rescan? That is usually where the pattern comes in.
  4. Pick the pattern (table below), then write the code.
  5. Test by hand with your edge cases before you hit submit.

cards.title: Spotting the pattern
cards.html:
The problem says... Try
"pair / two numbers that...", unsorted hashmap
sorted array, pair or triplet two pointers
contiguous subarray or substring, "longest/shortest with..." sliding window
subarray sum equals k, with negatives prefix sums + hashmap
"next greater/smaller", matching brackets stack (monotonic)
sorted, or "minimum value such that it works" binary search
top k, k-th largest, streaming median, merge k lists heap
all combinations / subsets / permutations backtracking
grid, islands, connected regions DFS/BFS on the grid
shortest path, fewest steps (unweighted) BFS
dependencies, ordering, "prerequisites" topological sort
"how many ways", "min cost", "can you reach", choices that overlap dynamic programming
intervals, meetings, ranges sort by start or end, then greedy

Self-check: n = 2 × 10⁵ and your plan has a nested loop. Will it pass? (No: 4 × 10¹⁰ operations. Look for O(n log n).)

levels.title: Recursion
levels.short: Base case, trust the call, memoisation

cards.title: Recursion
cards.html: Trees, backtracking, DFS and DP are all recursion. If recursion feels shaky, those four topics will too, so fix it here.

cards.title: The three questions
cards.html:
1. Base case: what's the smallest input whose answer you know immediately? (Empty list, None node, n == 0.)
  2. Smaller problem: how does the input shrink? (n - 1, node.left, nums[1:], index i + 1.)
  3. Combine: assuming the recursive call returns the right answer for the smaller problem, how do you build this answer from it?

Step 3 is the hard part to accept. Don't trace the whole call stack in your head. Assume the recursive call is correct and only check that one level is.

def depth(node):
    if node is None:               # 1. base case
        return 0
    left = depth(node.left)        # 2. smaller problems
    right = depth(node.right)
    return 1 + max(left, right)    # 3. combine

cards.title: Two styles
cards.html:
Return the answer (like depth above). This is cleanest when the answer for a node depends only on its children.

Accumulate into an outer variable when you need something global, such as a best-so-far or a list of results:

def all_paths(root):
    res = []
    def dfs(node, path):
        if not node:
            return
        path.append(node.val)
        if not node.left and not node.right:
            res.append(path[:])      # copy: path keeps changing
        dfs(node.left, path)
        dfs(node.right, path)
        path.pop()                   # undo before returning
    dfs(root, [])
    return res

To rebind an outer variable such as a number (best = max(best, x)), declare nonlocal best inside the inner function. Mutating an outer list (res.append) doesn't need it.

cards.title: Memoisation: recursion becomes DP
cards.html:
from functools import cache

@cache
def fib(n):
    if n < 2:
        return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)   # O(n) instead of O(2^n)

Arguments must be hashable (ints, strings, tuples; not lists).

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Passing nums[1:] copies the list on every call, so O(n²) overall. Pass an index instead.
  • Forgetting to return the recursive result: return helper(...), not just helper(...).
  • No base case, or a base case that's never reached, gives a RecursionError.

levels.title: The Refactorer
levels.short: Interview Python, recursion and the toolkit, with no hand-holding.

cards.title: Arrays & hashing
cards.html: The most common first step on LeetCode: trade O(n) memory for O(1) lookups and turn a nested loop into a single pass.

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
• "Find two numbers / a pair / a duplicate" in an unsorted array.
  • Counting, frequency, "anagram", "appears more than once".
  • Subarray sums, especially with negative numbers (prefix sums).

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
Seen-so-far lookup (one pass):

seen = {}                         # value -> index (or a set if you only need membership)
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    if target - x in seen:        # the partner we need
        return [seen[target - x], i]
    seen[x] = i

Group by a key:

groups = defaultdict(list)
for s in strs:
    groups[key_of(s)].append(s)   # key_of: tuple(sorted(s)), len(s), s[0], ...

Prefix sums:

prefix = [0]
for x in nums:
    prefix.append(prefix[-1] + x)
# sum of nums[i:j] == prefix[j] - prefix[i]   (O(1) per query)

To count subarrays with sum k: walk once, and at each step ask how many earlier prefixes equal current - k, using a dict of prefix counts that starts with {0: 1}.

cards.title: Why it works
cards.html: The brute force checks every pair, O(n²). The hashmap remembers everything you've passed, so "have I seen the partner?" is O(1), and one pass is enough.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Check for the partner before inserting the current element, or [3, 2, 4] with target 6 pairs the 3 with itself.
  • Lists aren't hashable. Use a tuple, or a string such as "#".join(...), as the key.
  • Counter(a) == Counter(b) is the one-line anagram check.

cards.title: Two pointers
cards.html: Two indexes moving through the array, usually from both ends inward, or one fast and one slow. Turns O(n²) pair-checking into O(n) on sorted data.

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
• Sorted array plus "pair / triplet that sums to...".
  • Palindromes, reversing in place.
  • "In place, O(1) extra space": remove duplicates, move zeroes, partition.

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
Opposite ends:

l, r = 0, len(a) - 1
while l < r:
    s = a[l] + a[r]
    if s == target:
        return [l, r]
    if s < target:
        l += 1        # need bigger: only l moving right can do that
    else:
        r -= 1        # need smaller

Read / write (same direction):

w = 0                       # next position to write
for r in range(len(a)):     # r reads everything
    if keep(a[r]):
        a[w] = a[r]
        w += 1
# a[:w] is the result

k-Sum: sort, fix the first number with a loop, then run opposite-ends on the rest. 3Sum is O(n²).

cards.title: Why it works
cards.html: On a sorted array, each comparison rules out a whole row of pairs. If a[l] + a[r] is too small, a[l] paired with anything left of r is also too small, so l can move on for good.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Skipping duplicates in 3Sum: skip equal i values, and after a match move l past equal values.
  • while l < r vs l <= r: for pairs you need two distinct elements, so <.
  • If the input isn't sorted and you sort it, you lose the original indexes (that's why Two Sum I uses a hashmap).

lc.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted

cards.title: Sliding window
cards.html: A window [l, r] that grows on the right and shrinks on the left, each pointer moving forward only. Every element enters and leaves once, so it's O(n).

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
• Contiguous subarray or substring.
  • "Longest / shortest / count of windows such that..." with a condition you can update incrementally (counts, sums, distinct characters).
  • Fixed size k: "max sum of k consecutive", "every window of size k".

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
Variable window (longest valid):

l = 0
best = 0
for r in range(len(s)):
    add(s[r])                    # grow the window
    while not valid():           # shrink until valid again
        remove(s[l])
        l += 1
    best = max(best, r - l + 1)

For shortest valid: shrink while it is valid, updating the best inside the while loop.

Fixed window of size k:

window = sum(a[:k])
best = window
for r in range(k, len(a)):
    window += a[r] - a[r - k]    # one in, one out
    best = max(best, window)

cards.title: Why it works
cards.html: Once a window [l, r] is invalid, every bigger window starting at l is invalid too, so l never has to move back. That one-directional property is what you must check before using a window.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Negative numbers break "sum ≤ k" windows: growing doesn't always increase the sum. Use prefix sums instead.
  • Window length is r - l + 1.
  • Keep window state in a Counter/defaultdict(int) or a set, and update it in both add and remove.

lc.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

cards.title: Stack
cards.html: A stack remembers things "until something resolves them". A monotonic stack keeps its contents sorted, so each element waits on the stack until the first element that beats it arrives.

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
• Matching pairs: brackets, tags, undo.
  • Evaluating expressions (RPN, calculators).
  • "Next greater element", "days until warmer", "how far can I see": anything asking for the nearest bigger or smaller item to the left or right.
  • Histogram and rectangle problems.

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
A Python list is a stack: append to push, pop() to pop, stack[-1] to peek, if stack: to check it isn't empty.

Next greater element (monotonic decreasing stack of indexes):

ans = [-1] * len(a)
stack = []                        # indexes still waiting for a bigger value
for i, x in enumerate(a):
    while stack and a[stack[-1]] < x:
        j = stack.pop()
        ans[j] = x                # or i - j for "how many steps until"
    stack.append(i)

Each index is pushed once and popped once, so the whole loop is O(n) despite the inner while.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Store indexes on the stack, not values, when you need distances or positions.
  • Always check if stack before stack[-1] or pop().
  • Strictly greater (<) vs greater-or-equal (<=) in the while condition changes how equal values behave. Read the problem.
  • Min Stack: push (value, current_min) pairs so the min is O(1).

levels.title: Binary search
levels.short: Sorted arrays and searching on the answer

cards.title: Binary search
cards.html: Halve the search space every step: O(log n). Works on sorted arrays, but also on any yes/no question whose answers flip once (False False False True True).

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
• Sorted (or rotated sorted) input and a target.
  • O(log n) required, or n up to 10⁹.
  • "Minimum speed / capacity / days such that it works" (binary search on the answer).

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
Find exact target:

lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] == target:
        return mid
    if a[mid] < target:
        lo = mid + 1
    else:
        hi = mid - 1
return -1          # lo is now where target would be inserted

First position where ok(x) is True (the most useful one):

lo, hi = smallest_possible, largest_possible
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if ok(mid):
        hi = mid          # mid might be the answer, keep it
    else:
        lo = mid + 1      # mid definitely isn't
return lo

Koko, ship capacity, split array: write ok(speed) as "can we finish in time at this speed?", then use the second template.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Infinite loops come from lo = mid with mid = (lo + hi) // 2. In the second template, only hi = mid is allowed; lo always moves to mid + 1.
  • Decide inclusive vs exclusive bounds once and stick with it.
  • Rotated arrays: compare a[mid] with a[hi] to see which half is sorted.
  • For plain lists, bisect_left/bisect_right already do this.

levels.short: Hashing, two pointers, sliding windows, stacks and binary search. Pick the right one.

cards.title: Linked lists
cards.html: Linked list problems are pointer bookkeeping. A handful of tricks cover almost all of them: dummy head, fast/slow pointers, in-place reversal.

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html: You're given head of a ListNode. That's it.

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

Dummy head: use it whenever the head itself might change (deleting, merging, inserting at the front).

dummy = tail = ListNode()
# ... tail.next = something; tail = tail.next
return dummy.next

Reverse in place:

prev, cur = None, head
while cur:
    cur.next, prev, cur = prev, cur, cur.next
return prev

(The one-liner is fine in Python because the right side is evaluated first. Write the 4-line version until it's automatic.)

Fast and slow:

slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
# slow is at the middle; if slow is fast at any point, there's a cycle

Gap of n: move fast n steps first, then move both. When fast hits the end, slow is n from the end.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Save cur.next before overwriting it.
  • while fast and fast.next: check both, or fast.next.next crashes.
  • Compare nodes with is, not ==.
  • Harder problems (Reorder List) are combos: find middle, reverse second half, merge.
  • LRU Cache = dict + doubly linked list. It's a favourite interview question.

lc.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

levels.title: Trees
levels.short: DFS returns, BFS levels, BST order

cards.title: Trees
cards.html: Almost every tree problem is either DFS with recursion (answer built from children) or BFS with a queue (level by level).

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
You're given root of a TreeNode. Then decide:

  • Answer depends on subtrees (depth, balanced, same tree, path sums): DFS, return values.
  • "Level", "row", "right side view", "minimum depth": BFS.
  • BST: inorder traversal is sorted. Use the ordering to skip half the tree.

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
DFS returning a value:

def dfs(node):
    if not node:
        return 0                       # value for an empty tree
    l, r = dfs(node.left), dfs(node.right)
    return combine(node.val, l, r)

DFS where the answer isn't what you return (diameter, max path sum): return height, but update an outer best with nonlocal.

BFS by level:

q = deque([root])
while q:
    for _ in range(len(q)):            # exactly one level
        node = q.popleft()
        ...
        if node.left:  q.append(node.left)
        if node.right: q.append(node.right)

Inorder (BST in sorted order):

def inorder(node):
    if node:
        yield from inorder(node.left)
        yield node.val
        yield from inorder(node.right)

Passing constraints down: for Validate BST, pass (lo, hi) bounds into children.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Handle root is None first.
  • Checking only parent-vs-child for BST validity is wrong; use bounds.
  • LCA in a BST: if both values are smaller, go left; both bigger, go right; otherwise you're at the LCA.
  • Inorder successor (the next node in sorted order) is the leftmost node of the right subtree, if there is one.

lc.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
Construct Tree from Preorder and Inorder

cards.title: Heaps
cards.html: A heap gives you the smallest item in O(1) and lets you insert or remove in O(log n). Whenever you need "the best few" out of many, or the best item while things keep changing, use a heap.

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
• "k-th largest / smallest", "top k", "k closest".
  • Merge k sorted things.
  • Always process the cheapest / earliest / largest next (schedulers, Dijkstra).
  • Running median (two heaps).

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
Top k with a size-k min-heap (O(n log k)):

heap = []
for x in nums:
    heapq.heappush(heap, x)
    if len(heap) > k:
        heapq.heappop(heap)      # throw away the smallest
# heap holds the k largest; heap[0] is the k-th largest

Max-heap: push -x, negate again when popping.

Heap of tuples: (priority, tie_breaker, item). Tuples compare left to right. If two priorities tie and the items aren't comparable (such as ListNodes), Python crashes, so add an index as the tie-breaker.

Merge k sorted lists:

heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
heapq.heapify(heap)
while heap:
    val, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
    ... # attach node; if node.next, push (node.next.val, i, node.next)

Median of a stream: max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half, kept within one of each other in size.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Python's heapq is a min-heap only.
  • heapq.heapify returns None; it works in place.
  • For "top k" you don't need a full sort (O(n log n)), but in an interview sorted(...)[:k] is fine to mention as the brute force.

lc.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
Kth Largest Element in an Array

cards.title: Backtracking
cards.html: Backtracking is DFS over choices: make a choice, recurse, then undo it. Use it when you must generate or search all combinations, and n is small (≤ 20 or so).

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
• "All subsets / permutations / combinations / partitions".
  • "Place N queens", Sudoku, word search in a grid.
  • Constraints are tiny, which hints at exponential time.

cards.title: Template
cards.html:
res = []
path = []

def backtrack(start):
    if is_complete(path):
        res.append(path[:])          # copy!
        return
    for i in range(start, len(choices)):
        if not allowed(choices[i]):
            continue
        path.append(choices[i])      # choose
        backtrack(i + 1)             # explore (i to allow reuse, i + 1 to forbid)
        path.pop()                   # un-choose

Variations come from three knobs:

Problem Start index Reuse? Record when
Subsets i + 1 no every node
Combinations / Combination Sum II i + 1 no target hit
Combination Sum i yes target hit
Permutations always 0, with a used array no len(path) == n

Duplicates in the input (Subsets II, Combination Sum II): sort first, then if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]: continue.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• res.append(path) without [:] stores the same list over and over, and it ends up empty.
  • Prune early (if remaining < 0: return, or break the loop once sorted candidates get too big).
  • Grid backtracking: mark the cell visited before recursing and restore it after.

lc.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number

cards.title: Graphs
cards.html: Graphs are nodes and edges. On LeetCode they usually arrive as a grid, an edge list, or an adjacency list. Three algorithms cover most problems: DFS/BFS traversal, topological sort, and union-find.

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
• Grid of cells, "islands", "regions", "spread": grid DFS/BFS.
  • "Fewest steps", "shortest path" with equal-cost moves: BFS.
  • "Prerequisites", "order of tasks", "is there a cycle in dependencies": topological sort.
  • "Connected components", "are these linked", adding edges one at a time: union-find.
  • Weighted shortest path: Dijkstra (heap + BFS).

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
Build an adjacency list:

graph = defaultdict(list)
for a, b in edges:
    graph[a].append(b)
    graph[b].append(a)    # only if undirected

Grid neighbours:

for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
    nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
    if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and ...:

BFS shortest path:

q = deque([(start, 0)])
seen = {start}
while q:
    node, dist = q.popleft()
    if node == goal:
        return dist
    for nxt in graph[node]:
        if nxt not in seen:
            seen.add(nxt)          # mark when pushing, not when popping
            q.append((nxt, dist + 1))

Topological sort (Kahn): count indegrees, queue every node with indegree 0, pop and decrement neighbours. If you processed fewer than n nodes, there's a cycle.

Union-find:

parent = list(range(n))
def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]   # path compression
        x = parent[x]
    return x
def union(a, b):
    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
    if ra == rb:
        return False        # already connected: this edge makes a cycle
    parent[ra] = rb
    return True

Dijkstra: heap = [(0, src)]; pop the closest; skip it if you've already finalised that node; push neighbours with d + w.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Mark visited when you enqueue, or nodes get queued many times.
  • Multi-source BFS (Rotting Oranges, Walls and Gates): put every source in the queue before starting.
  • Recursion depth on a 300×300 grid can pass 1000. Use BFS or an explicit stack if it crashes.

cards.title: Dynamic programming
cards.html: DP is recursion where the same sub-problems repeat, so you store their answers. Every DP problem is: define the state, write the recurrence, set the base cases, choose an order.

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
• "How many ways", "minimum cost", "maximum value", "is it possible".
  • Choices at each step whose effects overlap (rob this house or skip it; take this coin or not).
  • A greedy idea that almost works but you can find a counterexample.

cards.title: The recipe
cards.html:
1. State: what does dp[i] (or dp[i][j]) mean, in one sentence? ("Fewest coins to make amount i.")
  2. Recurrence: how is dp[i] built from smaller states? Think about the last decision.
  3. Base cases: dp[0], empty strings, first row and column.
  4. Order: fill so that every state you read is already computed. Return the cell that answers the question.

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
Top-down (easiest to write first):

from functools import cache

@cache
def best(i):
    if i >= len(nums):
        return 0
    return max(best(i + 1), nums[i] + best(i + 2))   # skip vs take
return best(0)

Bottom-up 1D:

dp = [0] * (n + 1)
dp[0] = base
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    dp[i] = f(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2], ...)

When dp[i] only uses the last two values, keep two variables instead of the array (O(1) space).

Bottom-up 2D (two strings / grid):

dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
for i in range(1, m + 1):
    for j in range(1, n + 1):
        if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
            dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
        else:
            dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])

cards.title: The common shapes
cards.html:
Shape Examples
Fibonacci-like dp[i-1], dp[i-2] Climbing Stairs, House Robber, Decode Ways
Unbounded choice over items Coin Change, Word Break, Combination Sum IV
0/1 knapsack Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum
Best ending at i LIS, Maximum Subarray
Two sequences dp[i][j] LCS, Edit Distance
Grid paths Unique Paths, Minimum Path Sum

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Write the brute-force recursion first, then add @cache. Convert to bottom-up only if you need to.
  • Off-by-one: with dp of size n + 1, dp[i] usually refers to the first i items, so the item itself is a[i - 1].
  • [[0] * n] * m again: always build 2D tables with a comprehension.

cards.title: Intervals & greedy
cards.html: Two related families. Intervals: almost always sort first, then sweep once. Greedy: make the locally best choice and prove (or convince yourself) it never hurts later.

cards.title: Spot it
cards.html:
• Pairs [start, end]: merge, insert, count overlaps, meeting rooms.
  • "Minimum number of X to remove / arrows / rooms".
  • Reachability with jumps; running sums that can reset (Kadane).

cards.title: Templates
cards.html:
Merge intervals:

intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
res = []
for s, e in intervals:
    if res and s <= res[-1][1]:
        res[-1][1] = max(res[-1][1], e)
    else:
        res.append([s, e])

Max non-overlapping set (activity selection): sort by end, keep each interval that starts after the last kept end.

Meeting rooms (how many overlap at once): sort starts and ends separately, or push end times onto a min-heap and pop any that finished before the next start. The heap size is the answer.

Kadane (max subarray):

best = cur = nums[0]
for x in nums[1:]:
    cur = max(x, cur + x)     # extend or restart
    best = max(best, cur)

Furthest reach (Jump Game): track reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]); fail if i > reach.

cards.title: How to trust a greedy
cards.html: Try to break it with small examples. If you can't find a counterexample after a few attempts, and you can explain in a sentence why swapping in your choice never makes things worse (the exchange argument), go with it. If you can break it, it's probably DP.

cards.title: Traps
cards.html:
• Sort by start for merging, by end for maximising the number kept.
  • Touching endpoints ([1,2] and [2,3]): read whether they count as overlapping.
  • Kadane: initialise with nums[0], not 0, or all-negative arrays break.

levels.title: The Grand Search
levels.short: Backtracking, graphs, DP and greedy: the hard end of the patterns.

cards.title: Practice system & beyond
cards.html: You've got the patterns. This stage is about doing problems under realistic conditions and remembering them a month later.

cards.title: The practice loop
cards.html:
1. Set a timer: 20 minutes for Easy, 35 for Medium, 50 for Hard.
  2. Use the routine from Big-O & approach: restate, brute force, find the waste, pick the pattern, code, test by hand.
  3. Stuck at the time limit? Read only the approach (not the code) of a good solution, close it, and write it yourself.
  4. After solving, write one line in your notes: the trick in plain words. ("Sort by end time; keep the earliest finisher.")
  5. Re-solve from scratch after 3 days and again after 2 weeks. If you can't, it goes back in the queue. This is where most of the learning happens.

cards.title: Rules of thumb
cards.html:
• Struggling with a problem for an hour and then reading the answer teaches less than 25 minutes of focused effort followed by the solution.
  • Mediums are where interviews live. Once a pattern's Easies feel routine, move on.
  • Re-solving a problem you've seen before is not cheating. Being able to recall a solution under pressure is a skill interviews test.
  • Talk out loud while you solve, even alone. Interviewers grade your reasoning, not only the final code.

cards.title: A mock interview (once a week)
cards.html: Pick a random Medium from a pattern you've finished. 45 minutes total: 5 to clarify and give examples, 5 to state the brute force and its complexity, 25 to code the optimal solution, 10 to test with edge cases and state final time/space. Talk through it out loud as if someone were listening.

cards.title: Beyond the core
cards.html:
These come up less often but still appear. Learn them once the 12 patterns feel solid:

  • Tries (prefix trees): autocomplete, word search with many words.
  • Bit manipulation: XOR tricks (a ^ a == 0), counting set bits, n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit.
  • Matrix manipulation: rotate, spiral, set zeroes. Mostly careful indexing.
  • Dijkstra (weighted shortest path) and Bellman-Ford (negative edges, limited stops).
  • Monotonic deque for sliding window maximum.

z1-q1.code:
x = 5
y = x
x = x + 2
print(x, y)
z1-q1.explain: y = x copies the value 5 into y. Changing x afterwards doesn't touch y.

z1-q2.explain: Anything inside {} in an f-string is worked out first, so {2 + 3} becomes 5.

z-hello.title: Say hello
z-hello.prompt: Read a name with input() and print Hello, NAME!
z-hello.starter: # read the name, then print the greeting
z-hello.hint: input() gives you a string. An f-string puts it in the sentence: f"Hello, {name}!"

z1-q3.code:
a = input()
b = input()
print(a + b)
z1-q3.explain: input() always returns a string. "3" + "4" glues the text together: "34". Use int(input()) for numbers.

z1-q4.prompt: Print the product of the two numbers.
z1-q4.explain: * multiplies. a and b are already numbers thanks to int().

z-add.title: Add two numbers
z-add.prompt: Read two whole numbers (one per line) and print their sum.
z-add.hint: input() always returns text, so "3" + "4" is "34". Wrap it: int(input()).
z-add.solution:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
print(a + b)

z1-q5.explain: 17 // 5 is how many whole 5s fit in 17 (3). 17 % 5 is what's left over (2).

z1-q6.explain: / always gives a float in Python 3, even when it divides evenly: 8 / 2 is 4.0.

z1-q7.title: Fix the bug
z1-q7.prompt: This should print how many whole hours are in the minutes, like 2 hours. It prints 2.0 hours. Fix it.
z1-q7.hint: Which division operator gives a whole number?
z1-q7.explain: / gives a float. // gives a whole number (rounded down).

z-minutes.title: Minutes to hours
z-minutes.prompt: Read a number of minutes and print it as H h M min. For 125 that's 2 h 5 min.
z-minutes.hint: // is whole-number division (125 // 60 is 2). % is the remainder (125 % 60 is 5).
z-minutes.solution:
minutes = int(input())
hours = minutes // 60
left = minutes % 60
print(f"{hours} h {left} min")

z-last-digit.title: Chop off the last digit
z-last-digit.prompt: Read a whole number (0 or more). Print its last digit, then on the next line print the number with that digit removed. For 1234: 4 then 123.
z-last-digit.hint: n % 10 is the last digit. n // 10 drops it. You'll use both constantly in the while-loop module.

z-receipt.title: Shop receipt
z-receipt.prompt: Read a price (like 2.5) and a quantity (a whole number). Print the total with exactly 2 decimal places.
z-receipt.hint: float() for decimals. In an f-string, {x:.2f} shows x with 2 decimal places (0.1 * 3 is really 0.30000000000000004).
z-receipt.solution:
price = float(input())
qty = int(input())
print(f"{price * qty:.2f}")

z2-q1.explain: Python runs only the first branch that's True. 72 >= 50 is True, so the elif is never checked. Put the stricter check first.

z2-q2.explain: The condition must be True exactly when n is below zero.

z-even-odd.title: Even or odd
z-even-odd.prompt: Read a whole number and print even or odd.
z-even-odd.hint: A number is even when n % 2 == 0. Remember the colon after the condition and the indent under it.

k-smallest.title: k smallest with a heap
k-smallest.prompt: Return the k smallest numbers in ascending order. Do it with heapq (either heapify + heappop k times, or heapq.nsmallest).
k-smallest.hint: heapify is O(n) and each heappop is O(log n), so this is O(n + k log n). Copy nums first so you don't mutate the input.
k-smallest.solution:
import heapq

def k_smallest(nums, k):
    heap = nums[:]
    heapq.heapify(heap)

subsets.title: Subsets
subsets.prompt: Return all subsets of a list of unique numbers, in any order.
subsets.hint: At index i, two choices: include nums[i] or don't. Record path[:] (a copy!) when i reaches the end.
subsets.solution:
def subsets(nums):
    res = []
    path = []

    def backtrack(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        path.append(nums[i])
        backtrack(i + 1)
        path.pop()
        backtrack(i + 1)

    backtrack(0)
    return res

permutations.title: Permutations
permutations.prompt: Return all permutations of a list of unique numbers, in any order.
permutations.hint: Choose any unused number, recurse, then undo the choice (pop and mark unused). The undo step is what makes it backtracking.
permutations.solution:
def permute(nums):
    res = []
    path = []
    used = [False] * len(nums)

    def backtrack():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            if not used[i]:
                used[i] = True
                path.append(x)
                backtrack()
                path.pop()
                used[i] = False

    backtrack()
    return res

flood-fill.solution:
def flood_fill(image, sr, sc, color):
    start = image[sr][sc]
    if start == color:
        return image
    rows, cols = len(image), len(image[0])

    def dfs(r, c):
        if 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols and image[r][c] == start:
            image[r][c] = color
            dfs(r + 1, c)
            dfs(r - 1, c)
            dfs(r, c + 1)
            dfs(r, c - 1)

    dfs(sr, sc)
    return image

course-schedule.title: Course Schedule
course-schedule.prompt: prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means take b before a. Return whether all courses can be finished (no cycle). Use Kahn's algorithm (BFS topological sort).
course-schedule.hint: Build an adjacency list b → a and count incoming edges. Start with all courses that have indegree 0. Each time you take one, decrement its neighbours. If you took every course, there's no cycle.
course-schedule.solution:
from collections import deque

def can_finish(num_courses, prerequisites):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]
    indegree = [0] * num_courses
    for a, b in prerequisites:
        graph[b].append(a)
        indegree[a] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(num_courses) if indegree[i] == 0)
    taken = 0
    while q:
        c = q.popleft()
        taken += 1
        for nxt in graph[c]:
            indegree[nxt] -= 1
            if indegree[nxt] == 0:
                q.append(nxt)
    return taken == num_courses

b5-1.title: Product except self
b5-1.prompt: Return a list where each position holds the product of every other number. No division, O(n).
b5-1.hint: Two passes: products of everything to the left, then multiply in everything to the right.
b5-1.solution:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return out

mistakes.title: Forgetting the colon
mistakes.why: Every line that starts a block (if, elif, else, for, while, def, class) ends with a colon.

mistakes.title: = instead of == in a condition
mistakes.why: One = stores a value. Two == compares. Conditions always compare.
mistakes.wrongErr: SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Maybe you meant '==' or ':=' instead of '='?

mistakes.title: Indentation that doesn't line up
mistakes.why: Python uses indentation to know what's inside a block. Use exactly 4 spaces per level, and line them up.

mistakes.title: A bracket that's never closed
mistakes.right: print("total:", (3 + 4))
mistakes.why: Count your brackets. The error often points at the line after the real mistake.

mistakes.title: Text without quotes
mistakes.right: print("hello")
mistakes.why: Without quotes, Python thinks hello is a variable name, and there isn't one.

mistakes.title: Treating input() as a number
mistakes.right:
age = int(input())
print(age + 1)
mistakes.why: input() always returns a string. Convert with int() or float() before doing maths.
mistakes.wrongErr: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

mistakes.title: Gluing text and a number with +
mistakes.right:
score = 42
print(f"Score: {score}")
mistakes.why: + joins two strings or adds two numbers, but not one of each. f-strings sidestep the problem.
mistakes.wrongErr: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

mistakes.title: Expecting / to give a whole number
mistakes.right: print(7 // 2)
mistakes.why: / always gives a float. // is whole-number division (it rounds down).

mistakes.title: // with negative numbers
mistakes.right: print(int(-7 / 2))
mistakes.why: // rounds down (towards minus infinity), so -3.5 becomes -4. To cut off the decimals towards zero, use int(a / b).

mistakes.title: Comparing floats with ==
mistakes.why: Floats are stored in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a small tolerance.

mistakes.title: int() on a decimal string
mistakes.right: print(int(float("3.5")))
mistakes.why: int() only accepts whole-number text. Go through float() first (it cuts off the decimal part).
mistakes.wrongErr: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.5'

mistakes.title: A while loop with no step
mistakes.right:
i = 0
while i < 3:
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
mistakes.why: If nothing in the body changes the condition, the loop never ends. Check that the loop variable moves every time round.

mistakes.title: Off by one with range
mistakes.right:
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)
mistakes.why: range stops before its stop value. To include n, write range(1, n + 1).

mistakes.title: x == a or b
mistakes.why: `day == 6 or 7` means `(day == 6) or 7`, and 7 on its own counts as True. Repeat the comparison, or write `day in (6, 7)`.

mistakes.title: Removing items from a list while looping over it
mistakes.right:
nums = [2, 4, 6, 7]
nums = [x for x in nums if x % 2 != 0]
print(nums)
mistakes.why: Removing shifts everything left, so the loop skips the next item. Build a new list instead.

mistakes.title: Expecting a for loop to change the list
mistakes.wrong:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
for x in nums:
    x = x * 10
print(nums)
mistakes.right:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
for i in range(len(nums)):
    nums[i] = nums[i] * 10
print(nums)
mistakes.why: x is a copy of each value. Assigning to it doesn't touch the list. Write to nums[i] (or build a new list).

mistakes.title: Indexing one past the end
mistakes.right:
s = "hello"
print(s[len(s) - 1], s[-1])
mistakes.why: Indexes run from 0 to len(s) - 1. s[-1] is the neat way to get the last item.
mistakes.wrongErr: IndexError: string index out of range

mistakes.title: Changing a character in a string
mistakes.right:
s = "hello"
s = "H" + s[1:]
print(s)
mistakes.why: Strings can't be changed in place. Make a new string (or work on list(s) and join it back).
mistakes.wrongErr: TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

mistakes.title: b = a doesn't copy a list
mistakes.right:
a = [1, 2]
b = a[:]
b.append(3)
print(a)
mistakes.why: Both names point at the same list. a[:] or list(a) makes a real copy.

mistakes.title: Building a grid with *
mistakes.right:
grid = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]
grid[0][0] = 1
print(grid)
mistakes.why: Multiplying the outer list repeats the same row object. Build each row separately.

mistakes.title: nums = nums.sort()
mistakes.right:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
nums.sort()
print(nums)
mistakes.why: .sort() sorts in place and returns None. Use nums.sort() on its own, or new = sorted(nums).

mistakes.title: Counting into a dict without a default
mistakes.why: A missing key raises KeyError. Use .get(key, 0), defaultdict(int) or Counter.

mistakes.title: Printing instead of returning
mistakes.wrong:
def double(x):
    print(x * 2)

result = double(4)
print("result is", result)
mistakes.right:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

result = double(4)
print("result is", result)
mistakes.why: A function without return gives back None. LeetCode checks what you return, never what you print.

mistakes.title: return inside the loop
mistakes.why: return ends the function immediately. Dedent it so it runs after the loop finishes.

mistakes.title: A list as a default argument
mistakes.wrong:
def add(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

add("a")
print(add("b"))
mistakes.right:
def add(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items

add("a")
print(add("b"))
mistakes.why: The default list is created once and shared by every call. Default to None and create the list inside.

mistakes.title: Naming a variable list, str, sum or max
mistakes.right:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(list("abc"))
mistakes.why: Using a built-in's name as a variable hides the built-in for the rest of the program.

mistakes.title: Recursion with no base case
mistakes.why: Every recursive function needs a case that returns without calling itself.

mistakes.title: Saving the path without copying it (backtracking)
mistakes.wrong:
res, path = [], []
def bt(i):
    if i == 2:
        res.append(path)
        return
    path.append(i)
    bt(i + 1)
    path.pop()
bt(0)
print(res)
mistakes.right:
res, path = [], []
def bt(i):
    if i == 2:
        res.append(path[:])
        return
    path.append(i)
    bt(i + 1)
    path.pop()
bt(0)
print(res)
mistakes.why: res ends up holding the same list object, which is empty once every pop has run. Append path[:].

mistakes.title: Checking `x in list` inside a loop
mistakes.wrong:
seen = []
for x in nums:
    if x in seen:      # scans the whole list every time
        return True
    seen.append(x)
mistakes.why: x in list is O(n), so doing it n times is O(n²). A set (or dict) lookup is O(1). This is the most common Time Limit Exceeded on LeetCode.

mistakes.title: Using list.pop(0) as a queue
mistakes.right:
from collections import deque
queue = deque([start])
while queue:
    node = queue.popleft()   # O(1)
mistakes.why: Removing from the front of a list moves everything else along. deque is built for it. BFS needs this.

mistakes.title: Building a big string with += in a loop
mistakes.right: out = " ".join(words)
mistakes.why: Strings can't change, so each += can copy the whole string so far. Collect pieces in a list and join once.

mistakes.title: Passing slices into recursion
mistakes.why: nums[1:] copies the list, so the whole thing becomes O(n²). Pass an index instead.

mistakes.title: "Modify nums in-place" but you reassign it
mistakes.wrong:
def sort_it(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)     # makes a new list, caller never sees it

data = [3, 1, 2]
sort_it(data)
print(data)
mistakes.right:
def sort_it(nums):
    nums.sort()              # or: nums[:] = sorted(nums)

data = [3, 1, 2]
sort_it(data)
print(data)
mistakes.why: When LeetCode says "do not return anything", it checks the list it passed you. Reassigning the name doesn't change that list; mutating it does.

mistakes.title: Forgetting the empty input
mistakes.why: Empty lists, empty strings, None heads and roots, n = 0: check them first. LeetCode's hidden tests always include them.

mistakes.title: Starting a max at 0
mistakes.wrong:
nums = [-5, -2, -8]
best = 0
for x in nums:
    best = max(best, x)
print(best)
mistakes.right:
nums = [-5, -2, -8]
best = float("-inf")
for x in nums:
    best = max(best, x)
print(best)
mistakes.why: If every value is negative, 0 wins wrongly. Start with nums[0] or float('-inf').
